title: Send Gate
user: A 2–10 person agency or trade business that needs a second pair of eyes on a quote or invoice before it reaches a client.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer asks which invoicing features matter and specifically seeks the workflows existing tools overcomplicate.
A self-hosted Invoice Ninja user requests submit/approve/deny states so a senior person can prevent duplicate or incorrect quotes and invoices from being sent.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 communities identify the same high-consequence moment: document creation is easy, but an accidental send harms a client relationship. It is most acute for small teams with junior administrators.
current_workaround: Draft in QuickBooks, Xero, Invoice Ninja, or a document editor; ask for approval over chat/email; then manually remember to send the final version.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, and Invoice Ninja create invoices, but formal approval is often a premium, broad-accounting feature. The unresolved gap is a tiny, auditable send gate that works with a PDF or a copied share link without adopting a new ledger.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first PWA that stores a quote/invoice PDF, recipient, amount, approver, and one approve/reject comment; it releases a final share/email draft only after approval. Non-goals: payment processing, bookkeeping, e-signatures, or a full CRM.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 5 of 8 teams route at least 20 documents through it and report zero accidental sends or duplicate sends.
monetization: one-time — the workflow has low ongoing infrastructure cost and small teams dislike another per-seat finance subscription.
constraints: Encrypt locally stored documents where supported; require explicit deletion controls; email sending should remain user-controlled; do not claim legal approval or accounting compliance.
why_distinct: It is a document-send checkpoint and handoff record, not another invoice generator or accounting package.

title: Retainer Ledger
user: Independent consultants and tradespeople who take deposits or retainers, then need to show exactly how later work draws down that money.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN discussion describes a freelance invoice as itemized milestones and incremental amounts due, rather than a single final bill.

A professional-services user explains that AP departments demand a numbered deposit invoice, but normal paid invoices cannot be cleanly drawn down against future progress invoices without manual credits or refunds.

recurrence: The pattern appears in both freelancer invoicing discussion and a detailed 2026 request from professional services/trades. Misstating a deposit as revenue or losing its balance creates client disputes and bookkeeping cleanup.
current_workaround: Issue a normal invoice, maintain a spreadsheet, and manually create credit notes or subtract the deposit from later invoices.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, and Invoice Ninja support invoices and payments, but the requester documents a missing lightweight distinction between a formal deposit request and earned work. The gap is an explainable, client-shareable drawdown trail.
smallest_useful_product: An offline ledger for one job: record a deposit request, payments, approved drawdowns, and remaining balance; export a branded one-page PDF statement. Non-goals: card collection, double-entry accounting, tax filing, or automatic revenue recognition.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users issue a statement for two or more jobs and can reconcile the displayed balance to their bank/payment record without a spreadsheet.
monetization: one-time — a local job-ledger utility can be bought when a business first needs deposits and should not tax every payment.
constraints: Use neutral wording such as “record,” not accounting advice; preserve immutable adjustment history; exported statements need a clear generated-at timestamp.
why_distinct: It manages the deposit-to-work explanation, a narrow layer absent from generic invoicing screens.

title: Split Cost Slip
user: Time-and-materials contractors who receive one supplier bill containing both their own costs and client-reimbursable items.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A startup operator asks how much reconciliation and invoice processing remains manual even when bookkeeping is outsourced.
A contractor describes one bank transaction containing subcontractor labor, equipment rental, and fuel; current 1:1 expense mapping forces duplicate expenses or lost billable/non-billable detail.

recurrence: Manual reconciliation appears in a general accounting discussion and in a concrete contractor request. The pain repeats for every mixed supplier invoice and directly affects what gets passed through to clients.
current_workaround: Enter the transaction once with a vague category, duplicate it into multiple expenses, or keep billable portions in a separate spreadsheet before recreating them on an invoice.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, Ramp, and Invoice Ninja cover expenses broadly; the unresolved small-business gap is a fast, receipt-first split that keeps an original total while producing a clean client reimbursement draft.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA where a user photographs or attaches one supplier bill, divides its total into named rows, marks each row billable/non-billable, and exports CSV plus a client-ready pass-through line list. Non-goals: bank sync, OCR guarantees, general ledger, or automatic tax categorization.
success_measure: Six of ten pilot contractors split 15+ mixed bills in a month and report that the row totals match every source bill without duplicate bookkeeping entries.
monetization: one-time — it is a focused companion to an existing accounting tool, not a hosted expense-management platform.
constraints: Make totals/rounding deterministic; retain original attachments locally; clearly label export categories as user-selected rather than tax advice.
why_distinct: The product’s primary artifact is one source bill split into billable and non-billable job costs, rather than another receipt scanner.

title: Performed For
user: Subcontractors, fractional specialists, and white-label agencies that bill a prime contractor but must identify the ultimate customer and engagement on each invoice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread on obtaining software-development contracts emphasizes the relationship-driven reality of agency and contractor work.
A detailed request says subcontractors currently bury the end client in project names or free text, leading to AP resend requests and no usable reporting across prime/end-client pairs.

recurrence: Contracting relationships are a recurring freelancer concern, and the 2026 request spells out the same need across consulting, staffing, MSP, creative, AEC, and advisory work.
current_workaround: Cram the end customer into a project name, use custom fields, add a note to the PDF, or maintain a separate spreadsheet mapping prime invoices to end engagements.
incumbents_and_gap: Invoice Ninja, QuickBooks, and Xero model the payer well but do not make “services performed for” a compact portable invoice field with a reusable relationship list. Full PSA/ERP products solve it at a complexity and price mismatch.
smallest_useful_product: A local invoice cover-sheet generator: choose billing client, end client, project/PO reference, and attach an existing invoice PDF to produce a clearly labeled companion page and CSV relationship report. Non-goals: contact CRM, invoicing, payment collection, or multi-level entity trees.
success_measure: In a 60-day pilot, 8 users produce 30+ cover sheets and fewer than 10% need a client to ask which end engagement an invoice belongs to.
monetization: one-time — the value is a reusable document layer around the billing product users already have.
constraints: Never imply the end client is liable for payment; avoid storing sensitive client details in a hosted service; preserve names/POs exactly as entered.
why_distinct: It fills the payer-versus-beneficiary identity gap without becoming a project-management or accounting system.

title: Deal Thread
user: A tiny business owner who needs to explain a quote’s path through partial delivery, invoice, credit, and payment without clicking through several systems.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster explicitly asks why invoice matching remains painful in 2026.
An ERPNext user says partial deliveries, returns, and multiple invoices require manually piecing documents, amounts, and dates together; they request one visual quotation-to-payment chain.

recurrence: Two 2026 discussions identify matching/tracing as still manual. It becomes severe once a straightforward job branches into a partial payment, revision, return, or second invoice.
current_workaround: Open quote, order, invoice, payment, and email records in separate tabs; manually compare numbers and annotate a spreadsheet or email thread.
incumbents_and_gap: ERPNext offers counts and document links, while accounting suites retain transactions. The gap is a simple importable relationship view for a one-person or tiny-team workflow—not an ERP implementation.
smallest_useful_product: A local graph/timeline tool that accepts CSV or manual entries for quote, invoice, payment, credit, and delivery; it flags unlinked amounts and exports a single PDF casefile. Non-goals: accounting sync, inventory fulfillment, payment initiation, or automated matching claims.
success_measure: Pilot users can answer ‘what happened to this quoted amount?’ in under two minutes for 80% of 20 sampled jobs, measured against their prior lookup time.
monetization: one-time — casefiles are occasional but important; local import avoids recurring integration costs.
constraints: Imports must tolerate malformed CSV; calculations must show source rows and never silently reconcile ambiguous sums; keep all transaction data on device by default.
why_distinct: The product is an explainable transaction narrative, not a replacement invoice, inventory, or ERP suite.

title: Due Board
user: A sole proprietor or household-sized business that needs a clean view of incoming supplier invoices, due dates, and manual payment status before cash arrives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small SaaS operator asks who handles bookkeeping and notes the practical difficulty of tracking receivables and payables.
A user asks for a simple due-date list of incoming invoices and a manual paid action; their workaround creates two transactions per invoice just to see an amount due.

recurrence: Payables visibility is raised independently in bookkeeping discussion and in a focused feature request. Missing a due date carries fees, supplier friction, and avoidable cash stress.
current_workaround: Use email flags, a calendar, spreadsheet, or a fake clearing account in a finance app; update payment status manually in more than one place.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, and Firefly III have broad payables/transactions, but their setup is disproportionate for someone who only needs a local list of bills to pay and a proof-of-payment note.
smallest_useful_product: An offline due-date board with supplier, amount, due date, attachment, paid date, and a weekly printable list. Non-goals: bank connections, bill payment, OCR, accounting journal entries, and credit scoring.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilots enter ten bills in the first month and can account for every due/paid status in a weekly review without opening their inbox.
monetization: free — a no-account local utility is a credible acquisition wedge; optional export/templates can later be paid.
constraints: Dates/time zones must be unambiguous; attachments stay local; provide data export and a deletion path; no financial advice or payment guarantees.
why_distinct: It intentionally stops at bill awareness and payment recording instead of recreating full accounts payable software.

title: Deadline Packet
user: Freelancers earning cross-border income who need a calm, accountant-ready packet of invoices, receipts, deadline notes, and unanswered questions for a specific filing period.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Indian freelancers and contractors describe juggling spreadsheets, accountant WhatsApp messages, and deadline panic for GST, TDS, FEMA, and CA coordination.
A self-hosted invoice user asks for an EU in-memory, no-storage alternative to a third-party receipt/invoice extraction provider, signaling privacy constraints around document preparation.

recurrence: The HN thread reports multiple freelancers with fragmented compliance coordination; the separate 2026 request confirms that handling invoice/receipt documents through third parties is a trust concern.
current_workaround: Keep spreadsheets, scattered scans, calendar reminders, and a WhatsApp/email conversation with an accountant; compile files hurriedly near deadlines.
incumbents_and_gap: Tally, Zoho Books, ClearTax, Xero, and accountants address ledgers or filings. The gap is a local, jurisdiction-template-neutral ‘here is what my accountant needs’ evidence packet that does not masquerade as filing software.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first checklist builder with filing-period folders, attachments, a missing-evidence list, and a zipped/PDF index for accountant handoff. Non-goals: calculating tax, submitting returns, legal advice, OCR-as-truth, or government integrations.
success_measure: In pilots, 70% of users complete a packet at least seven days before their stated deadline and their accountant requests fewer than two follow-up documents on average.
monetization: one-time — privacy-sensitive users should be able to prepare and export a packet without a data-retention subscription.
constraints: No country-specific legal claims without qualified review; encrypt local files where available; make retention and export explicit; never send documents automatically to accountants.
why_distinct: It organizes evidence and questions for human review rather than pretending to automate compliance or being a thin OCR/LLM wrapper.

title: Gentle Chase
user: A freelancer or family business owner who wants consistent, relationship-aware follow-up for overdue invoices without handing customer data to an automated debt-collection service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A founder says overdue chasing is manual and awkward; small businesses either rely on QuickBooks/Xero reminders, send WhatsApp manually, or let it slide to protect the relationship.
A user requests customer treatment conditional on having no unpaid recurring invoices, showing that payment status needs to feed deliberate client communication and policy.

recurrence: The HN discussion explicitly describes multiple existing workarounds, and a separate invoice-system request links payment status to customer treatment. The harm is inconsistent collection and uncomfortable client interactions.
current_workaround: Hope an accounting-suite reminder works, write ad hoc WhatsApp/email messages, or avoid following up until the balance is seriously overdue.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks/Xero reminders and debt-collection tools are either generic or overly escalatory. The gap is a private cue-and-draft system that preserves a human decision at every send.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA with invoice amount/due date, contact preference, follow-up cadence, notes, and editable email/WhatsApp copy buttons; it never sends messages itself. Non-goals: payment processing, debtor scoring, automated messaging, collections, or legal notices.
success_measure: After 60 days, pilot users record a follow-up for 85% of invoices overdue by seven days and report fewer than 10% of follow-ups were missed because they forgot.
monetization: one-time — the user keeps control and data local; there is no messaging infrastructure to justify a recurring charge.
constraints: No automatic contact or harassment features; provide jurisdiction-neutral templates only; store client notes locally and offer export/delete.
why_distinct: It supports the awkward human follow-up decision rather than becoming an AI collection agent or a generic invoice app.

title: Shift Chain
user: A solo service provider coordinating a handful of dependent client jobs who needs downstream promises to update when an earlier appointment slips.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solopreneur scheduling discussion reports that Calendly-style tools are too rigid for changing availability, overkill for simple coordination, and often awkward on mobile.
An ERPNext user says real task completion changes downstream dates, but current planning requires manually adjusting every dependent timeline.

recurrence: Scheduling rigidity appears in both solo-business and project-planning contexts. The pain is repeated rescheduling after ordinary variability, not discovering another calendar provider.
current_workaround: Edit calendar events individually, maintain a separate task list, message each affected client manually, or buy an over-featured scheduling/project suite.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly and Cal.com center booking; Asana and ERPNext center broader projects. The gap is a deliberately small mobile-friendly dependency chain that proposes—not silently performs—schedule changes.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA with named jobs, durations, dependencies, buffers, and a ‘job moved’ action that lists downstream proposed dates plus copyable client updates. Non-goals: public booking pages, calendar sync, team resource planning, or route optimization.
success_measure: A pilot user reschedules 15 dependent jobs and accepts or edits a proposed plan in under five minutes in at least 80% of cases.
monetization: one-time — it is a lightweight companion for variable service work, without hosted calendar infrastructure.
constraints: Never alter an external calendar automatically; clearly distinguish proposed from confirmed dates; all client contact text remains editable.
why_distinct: It handles the ripple effect after a change, which booking links and generic task lists leave to manual coordination.

title: Stock Promise
user: A small distributor or reseller taking orders in parallel who needs to avoid promising the same scarce item twice while an order is still being entered.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An e-commerce operator asks how businesses handle reconciliation across Shopify, payment providers, and accounting systems and which part is most frustrating.
A wholesale distributor describes 36 agents entering thousands of multi-line phone orders; stock is not protected until save, so the same SKU can be promised to more than one customer.

recurrence: Both 2026 threads expose the operations-to-records seam in commerce. The ERPNext request provides a concrete high-severity example: a promised item can become unavailable before order completion.
current_workaround: Tell staff to refresh inventory manually, save incomplete orders, write temporary reservations in chat/spreadsheets, or use a heavyweight ERP customization.
incumbents_and_gap: Shopify and ERPNext track inventory, but the cited gap is an explicit temporary commitment while an order is still in progress. Large OMS/ERP systems solve it with far more process than small resellers need.
smallest_useful_product: A small local-network web app for a shared SKU list: staff create a timed, visible soft hold with customer/order note; a supervisor converts, releases, or expires it; CSV export records the outcome. Non-goals: e-commerce storefronts, warehouse management, purchasing, accounting sync, or multi-warehouse forecasting.
success_measure: Across a two-week pilot, 95% of contested SKUs are either converted or released before expiry, with zero known duplicate promises for held stock.
monetization: subscription — reliable shared live holds, accounts, and expiry notifications require a hosted coordination service.
constraints: Use atomic server-side hold creation and expiry; avoid presenting soft holds as legal reservations; maintain an append-only audit log; scope v1 to a single location.
why_distinct: It is the missing pre-save promise layer, not a clone of a storefront, POS, or full inventory system.

title: Request Sheet
user: A service business with repeat clients who needs clients to request a priced or price-on-ask quote without exposing a full storefront or forcing a portal migration.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer building an invoicing platform asks what belongs in a freelancer-specific workflow and calls out the bloat of tools aimed at broader small businesses.
A self-hosted user asks for clients to select available products in the portal, request quotes, or generate/pay an invoice; they call API-based assembly an unnecessary UX detour.

recurrence: A freelancer-specific invoicing discussion and a 2026 client-portal request both push against bloated systems for a simple repeat-client request flow.
current_workaround: Take requests by email or WhatsApp, copy line items into a quote, or build a storefront/API integration that is excessive for a few services or custom jobs.
incumbents_and_gap: Shopify handles retail storefronts; Invoice Ninja has a portal; service CRMs add broad workflow. The open space is an intentionally constrained request sheet that turns client selections into a human-reviewed quote draft.
smallest_useful_product: A static, shareable service/product request form with allowed items, quantities, free-text requirements, and a downloadable quote-draft CSV/PDF for the owner. Non-goals: checkout, live inventory, client accounts, payment collection, CRM, or automatic quote acceptance.
success_measure: At least half of repeat-client requests arrive through the sheet in a 30-day pilot, and owners produce a quote draft in under three minutes for 80% of them.
monetization: freemium — a free hosted/shareable sheet can spread through small businesses; branded templates and exports are a clear paid upgrade.
constraints: No implied binding price or stock availability; keep contact collection minimal; make form data exportable/deletable; support accessibility and mobile use.
why_distinct: It captures the request-to-quote handoff without turning into another retail site, CRM, or invoicing platform.

title: Work Receipt
user: Freelancers billing for modern knowledge work who need an honest, privacy-preserving client-readable record of what was done and when, including AI-assisted work.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer says AI-agent prompting, review, and waiting make app-based tracking unconvincing; increasingly accurate tracking also becomes increasingly tedious.
A local-first finance-app user reports that an offline transaction write persists but is not visible until reload, showing why offline work records must make local saves immediately legible.

recurrence: The HN thread is a current, direct pain statement about accurately billing AI-era work. The independent 2026 local-first finance issue reinforces that people expect immediately visible, durable local records rather than opaque syncing behavior.
current_workaround: Run a timer, estimate after the fact, infer time from Git branches, or produce a manually written status update alongside an invoice.
incumbents_and_gap: Toggl and Harvest optimize timers; Invoice Ninja focuses on billing. The gap is a small client-facing work receipt that allows a freelancer to declare sessions, outcomes, interruptions, and evidence links without surveillance screenshots.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA with start/stop/manual sessions, project/outcome notes, optional links to commits/files, and a branded weekly PDF receipt for attachment to an invoice. Non-goals: employee surveillance, keystroke capture, screenshots, payroll, automatic activity inference, or invoicing.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, users attach a work receipt to 75% of hourly invoices and spend under five minutes per week correcting records.
monetization: one-time — privacy-preserving local proof should work without a per-seat surveillance subscription.
constraints: Never collect activity data by default; preserve user control over every client-visible note/link; be clear that a receipt is self-reported, not independent verification.
why_distinct: It creates a humane invoice attachment for outcome-based explanation, not another timer or invasive monitoring product.
